title: Replace, Rebuild or Run It Longer: The Canadian Fleet Equipment Call for 2027
summary: Tariffs on U.S. trailers, a 100% write-off proposal, firm used values and Ontario emissions tests. How Canadian fleets should replace, rebuild or run in 2027.
body_markdown:
Unit 214 comes in on a hook at 6:15 on a Tuesday morning in November.


It's a 2019 sleeper with just over 1.1 million kilometres on it. The driver got an aftertreatment warning eastbound on the 401, then a derate, then a long wait on the shoulder near Woodstock. Another truck recovered the load. That bill hasn't landed yet.


You run maintenance for a 70-tractor dry van and reefer fleet in southwestern Ontario, with a satellite yard in Quebec. By ten, your lead tech's diagnosis is on your desk. The aftertreatment needs major work, and the oil analysis makes a rebuild conversation unavoidable.


You've got three options. Rebuild it and run it three more years. Sell it and replace it. Or patch it and push the call into 2027.


You're made up for this story. The decision isn't. Maintenance leads across Canada are staring at some version of unit 214 this winter, and the math behind it moved more this fall than in the three years before.


## Why running it longer isn't the cheap option anymore


Running an older truck used to be the safe default. Defer the capital, keep the kilometres going, fix failures as they come.


That logic breaks when downtime gets expensive. Statistics Canada's for-hire motor carrier freight services price index hit 133.0 in the second quarter of 2026 (released Aug. 31). That's up 5.3% from the first quarter and about 9.5% from a year earlier.


What it means for you: freight is paying more, so a tractor sitting in a bay for nine days is missing better loads than it would have a year ago. A breakdown now costs the repair plus the revenue the truck didn't earn.


Then there's the shop itself. In a national trucking workforce survey of 57 senior leaders, released Oct. 2, 2026, 58% said technician roles were hard to fill. Only company drivers ranked harder.


"Run it longer" assumes you have the bay time and the hands. If your techs are stretched, every extra failure on an aging truck pushes PMs back on the rest of the fleet.


And the province is watching the exhaust.


In Ontario, a diesel commercial vehicle with a registered gross weight over 4,500 kg needs an emissions test once it's at least seven model years old and you're renewing the plate sticker. A 2019 unit like 214 is already there. Model year 2011 and newer trucks fail above 10% opacity, a limit in force since July 1, 2023. Fail, and the plate doesn't get renewed until the truck passes.


So unit 214's aftertreatment isn't optional. It's a registration problem with a date attached.


The Quebec yard has its own clock. The SAAQ requires maintenance at least every six months on vehicles with a GVWR of 4,500 kg or more, and says the periodic mechanical inspection doesn't replace it. Older equipment doesn't change those rules. It just makes them harder to pass on the first try.


If running longer costs more, the obvious move is to buy. That's where the border comes in.


## What replacement costs once the border gets involved


Most of the equipment in your yard was built somewhere else. That used to be a footnote. Now it's a line item.


Start with trucks. U.S. Proclamation 10984, issued Oct. 17, 2025, put a 25% Section 232 tariff on imported medium and heavy-duty trucks and key parts, including engines, transmissions and tires, from Nov. 1, 2025. For USMCA-qualifying trucks, it applies only to non-U.S. content.


That's a U.S. duty. But you buy in the same North American market and feed your trucks from the same parts supply chain. Component costs don't stay politely south of the border.


Trailers hit closer to home.


Canada's United States Surtax Order (2026) took effect Sept. 8, 2026, with surtaxes of 15%, 25% or 50% on listed U.S.-origin goods, per the Canada Border Services Agency's Customs Notice 26-23. Goods-transport trailers under tariff items 8716.39.10 through 8716.39.90 sit on the 25% schedule. Highway tractors don't appear in the schedules.


What that means for you: a U.S.-built van or reefer you import now can carry a 25% surtax on its value for duty. A Canadian-built one doesn't.


The relief window just narrowed, too. On Nov. 9, 2026, the Department of Finance extended its horizontal remission for U.S. goods to June 30, 2028, but said that relief ends for certain trailers on Dec. 1, 2026, citing domestic production. Case-by-case remission is still possible. It's a request, not a default, so talk to your customs broker before you count on it.


Then there's the engine. EPA's 2027 NOx rule stands, and its July 2026 amendments on warranty and penalties were still a proposal in mid-November trade reporting. Environment and Climate Change Canada's interim order of Oct. 13, 2026 (published in the Canada Gazette Oct. 31) keeps EPA-certified model year 2027 trucks importable here, and final U.S. changes would apply while it's in force.


Buyers are reading the same fog. Two industry forecasters put October 2026 North American Class 8 orders at 13,500 units (down 45% year over year) and 15,600 units (down 36%), blaming unclear 2027 rules and costs.


Money isn't getting cheaper, either. On Oct. 28, 2026, the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate to 2.5% and said further hikes could be needed. The next decision is Dec. 9, and every unit you finance in 2027 carries that rate path.


So replacement is pricier and murkier. But Ottawa just changed the after-tax side.


## The write-off that changes the math


Freight trucks rated above 11,788 kg sit in CCA Class 16 at 40% declining balance. Trailers fall in Class 10 at 30%.


Under the reaccelerated investment incentive, the CRA says qualifying property acquired from Jan. 1, 2025 gets an enhanced first-year claim. Available for use before 2030, that's generally triple the normal half-year amount. On a Class 16 tractor, 60% in year one instead of 20%.


Then, on Sept. 15, 2026, the federal government proposed the Productivity Mega Deduction. It would allow a permanent 100% write-off, in the year the asset becomes available for use, for most depreciable property acquired on or after Sept. 15, 2026.


The exclusions cover most buildings, goodwill and certain Class 10 and 10.1 vehicles like passenger cars and some pickups. Class 16 freight trucks aren't on that list. Used property can qualify, unless you or a non-arm's-length party owned it before.


Two cautions. It's draft legislation, not law. And the deduction lands in the year the unit goes into service, not when you sign the order. A tractor waiting on a spring build slot lands in a different tax year.


The rebuild has its own question. CRA separates repairs that restore a property from capital spending that gives a lasting benefit. Settle where an in-frame lands with your accountant before the work order opens.


What it means for you: the after-tax gap between rebuilding and replacing has narrowed for tractors. It hasn't for a U.S.-built trailer carrying a surtax.


## What your old trucks will fetch


Replacing has a second half: what the outgoing unit is worth.


A November 2026 Canadian used-truck market report, covering October, found used sleeper inventory down 32.7% year over year. Day cab auction values rose 7.3% from September. The same publisher's August report had sleeper auction values up 7% year over year.


Translated: far fewer used sleepers are for sale than a year ago, and buyers are paying up. Even with known problems, unit 214 sells into a thin market. That won't last forever, but it's real this quarter.


Supply is tight for a reason. An aftermarket research firm reported in January 2026 that Canadian Class 8 sales fell 11% in 2025, with 1% growth expected this year. And a fleet management firm's 2026 survey found about 30% of Canadian operators delaying or extending replacement cycles, versus 22% in the U.S.


Your peers are holding. That's why their trucks aren't hitting the used market.


## Making the call on unit 214


Back to the desk. You don't decide unit 214 alone. You decide it against every unit in the yard.


**Rebuild** when the chassis is sound, the unit runs lanes where an older truck isn't a service risk, and the shop has bay time. The rebuild should cost clearly less than what the truck fetches today plus a replacement's after-tax cost. Rebuild a truck that then fails its emissions test, and you've bought the worst of both options.


**Replace** when the unit shows a pattern, not one event. Look for repeat aftertreatment faults, rising cost per kilometre over 12 months, and a test or inspection coming due. A tight used market pays you for your problem child.


**Run longer** for clean, lower-kilometre units on short-haul or yard work. Put them there on purpose, not by default.


Here's how it plays out. Unit 214 sells as-is into the thin sleeper market. A stock tractor already on a dealer lot replaces it, in service before year end. Two other 2019 units with clean oil analysis get aftertreatment work, a fresh emissions test and three more years on regional runs.


The trailer order splits. Canadian builds get quoted against U.S. builds with the 25% surtax and the lost Dec. 1 relief priced in.


None of that came from a fleet average. It came from the unit records.


## Put the decision in the system, not a spreadsheet


Every fleet's replacement threshold is different. A Montreal to Toronto reefer fleet, a northern Alberta flatbed outfit and a dedicated retail operation in the Lower Mainland shouldn't run the same rule. Serious shops encode their own in the systems dispatch, maintenance and billing all touch.


That's where a configurable TMS and maintenance workflow earns its keep: unit-level fields, statuses dispatch respects, approval permissions and cost-per-kilometre views tied to the unit and the lanes it ran.


Build this before January:


-


**Unit records with decision dates:** model year, Ontario emissions test due, inspection sticker expiry, Quebec six-month maintenance due, warranty end.


-


**Trailing 12-month cost per kilometre by unit,** with repairs, tows, recovery loads and downtime allocated to the truck, not buried in overhead.


-


**Statuses for the in-between:** "replacement candidate," "rebuild approved," "pending sale," so planners stop assigning long runs to a unit you're selling.


-


**Approval rules by dollar threshold,** so nobody opens an in-frame without the person who owns the replace decision signing off.


-


**Origin, CCA class and in-service date on every purchase,** so surtax and tax timing show up in the comparison, not in a surprise.


When the data lives there, unit 214 isn't a debate. It's a report.


## The takeaway


Replace, rebuild or run longer isn't a fleet-wide policy for 2027. It's a unit-by-unit call, and the inputs shifted this fall.


Downtime costs more because freight pays more. Ontario's emissions test turns old aftertreatment into a plate deadline. U.S.-built trailers carry a 25% surtax, and broad relief ends Dec. 1. The proposed 100% write-off tilts tractor math toward replacing, if the unit is in service in the right year. And scarce used sleepers will pay you for the trucks you let go.


Put the dates, costs and statuses on every unit record. Then let the records make the call.


## FAQ


### Are U.S.-built trailers subject to Canada's counter-tariffs?


Yes, U.S.-origin trailers under tariff items 8716.39.10 to 8716.39.90 carry a 25% surtax under the United States Surtax Order (2026), effective Sept. 8, 2026. Horizontal remission for them ends Dec. 1, 2026, though case-by-case remission requests remain open.


### Does Canada's counter-tariff list include highway tractors?


No, the order's schedules don't list highway tractor tariff items. Tractors can still carry indirect costs from the 25% U.S. Section 232 tariff on imported trucks and key parts in effect since Nov. 1, 2025.


### Can I write off a new tractor 100% in the first year?


Possibly, if the proposed Productivity Mega Deduction becomes law; it would cover most property acquired on or after Sept. 15, 2026, in the year it's available for use. Until then, the reaccelerated investment incentive gives a Class 16 truck about 60% in year one.


### When does an Ontario truck need an emissions test?


A diesel commercial vehicle over 4,500 kg registered gross weight needs one at plate renewal once it's at least seven model years old, or on a change of owner if it's older than the current model year. Without a pass, the plate won't be renewed.


### Does Quebec's mechanical inspection replace preventive maintenance?


No, the SAAQ says periodic mechanical inspection doesn't replace mandatory maintenance, which is due at least every six months on vehicles with a GVWR of 4,500 kg or more.
